failure_analysis.what_failed: The supervisor chases oscillating (sine) disturbances. It derives the load d1/d2 from the instantaneous upper-level flows, so during a few-minute sine these estimates reverse every ~150 s. The setpoint bias then swings in phase, but the base PI loops need 90-120 s to settle, so production never converges (large integral off-target) and the self-inflicted setpoint excursions drive h3 over 0.75 m and h2 out of band.
failure_analysis.next_recommendation: After this, consider a shorter-horizon filter used only for the fast upper-level/saturation guard, or a consistency/hysteresis test on the smoothed load, to recover step-response speed without re-introducing sine chasing.

self_check: By averaging the load and gain estimates over the last 240 s, the setpoint bias follows the persistent mean load; for a zero-mean sine the mean is ~0 so the setpoints stay near nominal, Q stays on target, and the self-inflicted h3/h4 excursions vanish. For sustained steps or ramps the mean converges to the true load, so the candidate model still shifts the h1/h2 split along the constant-Q curve whenever the predicted h3p/h4p exceed the limit or the predicted pump voltages exceed 12 V. The 240 s averaging also dilutes the supervisor's own setpoint transients, so the residual transient-driven estimate error is small. Thus production is held by the base loops while constraint protection acts on the sustained component only.
proposed_change: Replace the instantaneous (last-sample) load and gain estimates with moving averages over the last 240 samples, so the setpoint bias responds to the persistent mean load instead of the oscillating component.

failure_analysis.what_failed: The worst scenarios are all the oscillatory (sine) feed/combined ones. The supervisor estimates d1,d2 from a single-sample steady-state mass balance and then re-solves and moves the split every 10 s, i.e. at a rate comparable to (even faster than) the 1.5-2 min inner-loop settling time. On a zero-mean sinusoidal feed disturbance this makes the outer loop chase, out of phase, and amplify the plant swing: production runs from 14.85 to 17.54 L/s, setpoint travel grows past 1 m, h2 dips below the 0.25 band and h3 crosses 0.75 m while v1/v2 slam into the 12 V rail. The static estimator also ignores dh/dt, so during transients it reports a disturbance biased toward the level rate rather than the true load.
failure_analysis.next_recommendation: If the slow observer is not enough on long-period oscillations, add explicit oscillation detection (zero-crossing count of the smoothed residual over the window) that freezes or heavily damps the split while the swing persists.

self_check: The observer replaces the single-sample mass-balance residual with a first-order low-pass of that residual over the whole 600 s window (tau = 120 s), so a zero-mean sinusoidal load produces almost no net bias and the supervisor stops chasing it, leaving the inner PI loops to regulate the levels; a sustained step or ramp still propagates through in roughly 2-3 minutes, which is slightly slower than the inner-loop settling time. Because the same smoothed d1,d2 feed the pump-flow inversion and the v>12 V / h3,h4>limit penalties, a persistent load is still transferred off the saturating pump and off the tank whose upper level is climbing toward 0.75 m. The existing 0.06 m per-call step limit caps travel, so the slower observer cannot introduce large setpoint jumps.
proposed_change: Replace the single-sample disturbance estimate used for the split with a first-order low-pass filter (tau = 120 s) of the instantaneous mass-balance residual, applied across the telemetry window, so the outer loop is slower than the inner PI loops and stops chasing zero-mean oscillations.

failure_analysis.what_failed: The supervisor estimates the load (d1,d2) and the pump gains from the single last sample. Under sinusoidal feed/pump/split disturbances the instantaneous estimate flips sign with the oscillation phase, so the constant-Q operating point is chased back and forth along the curve. Each move injects a 1.5-2 min PI transient (off-target production) and the resulting corner splits (e.g. sp=[0.403,0.240]) push h2 below its band and raise the opposite upper level above 0.75 m (h3=0.765, h4=0.85). Step/ramp cases react only once, so they are not the problem; the score is dominated by the sinusoidal scenarios.
failure_analysis.next_recommendation: Keep the single windowed load/gain estimator; next, if a type still regresses, make the averaging window adaptive (long only when the load estimate is oscillatory, short otherwise) so step/ramp response is not delayed.

self_check: The load estimate d1,d2 and the pump-gain estimate are now computed from 3-minute window averages of h1..h4 and v1,v2 instead of the last sample, so an oscillating disturbance is seen as its mean and the chosen constant-Q split stops chasing the oscillation phase; the PI loops keep Q on target with a steady split. Because production is set by the h1/h2 setpoints alone, the only reason to move the split is to keep a pump out of saturation or to hold h3/h4 under the limit, and the averaged estimate still tracks the mean of a biased disturbance so those constraints are met with far fewer, smaller setpoint moves (less travel, fewer transients, no corner splits that pushed h2 out of band or h3/h4 over the limit).
proposed_change: Replace the single-sample load (d1,d2) and pump-gain estimates with averages over the most recent 180 one-second samples, so oscillating disturbances drive the mean split instead of chasing the oscillation phase.

failure_analysis.what_failed: The supervisor estimates disturbances and pump flows from steady-state mass balances that ignore tank level rates of change. During oscillating feed disturbances, this missing accumulation term causes a phase-lagged and biased disturbance estimate, so the split is shifted the wrong way, violating the h2 band and upper level limits and driving large production errors and setpoint travel.
failure_analysis.next_recommendation: Use the full dynamic mass balances, including dh/dt for all four tanks, to estimate d1, d2 and the pump flows A and B, instead of the steady-state relations that neglect accumulation.

self_check: By including dh/dt in the mass balances, the supervisor sees the true disturbance even while levels are moving, so an oscillating feed is detected in phase rather than as a delayed bias. The split then moves early enough to keep h3/h4 below the limit and h2 inside its band, while the existing cost still penalises setpoint travel and pump saturation. Steady-state behaviour is unchanged because derivatives vanish there, and the pump-gain estimates are recomputed from the dynamic flows with the same clamping.
proposed_change: Replace the steady-state disturbance and pump-flow estimates with dynamic mass-balance estimates that include the measured tank level rates of change dh/dt.

failure_analysis.what_failed: The worst scenarios are the sinusoidal disturbances (feed, split, pump and combined sines). The supervisor re-evaluates the instantaneous mass-balance load residual every ~45 s and moves the setpoints by 0.05-0.10 m along the constant-Q curve each time, while the PI loops need ~120 s to settle. So the setpoint commands chase the oscillation instead of the disturbance mean: every move injects a lagged production transient (Q swings +/-1 L/s, matching 14 L/s per metre of setpoint move), drives h2 transiently out of [0.25,0.45], and pushes h3 above 0.75 through the tank3 inflow needed to raise h1. The step/ramp scenarios are cheap (30-160) precisely because the instantaneous estimate is correct there, which is why the earlier attempts that low-pass filtered or averaged the residual always lost on the steps: the delayed estimate let h3 run past its limit before the split was corrected.
failure_analysis.next_recommendation: Keep the instantaneous residual for step/ramp loads but detect sustained oscillation from the residual series itself and, only then, use the residual median so the outer split loop stops chasing a zero-mean disturbance.

self_check: The load residual over the 10-minute window is classified: a persistent step or ramp stays on one side of its own median (<=2 sign reversals), so the fast instantaneous residual is used and h3/h4 are pulled back before they reach the 0.75 m limit. A sustained oscillation reverses sign three or more times, so the split is computed from the residual median, i.e. the mean load, which holds h1/h2 near the constant-Q operating point and stops injecting setpoint transients that push h2 out of band or a pump into the 12 V rail. Because the switch only changes the load estimate, the step response of the base layer is untouched. All setpoint moves remain limited to 0.06 m per call and the loops are left to settle, so the split is only moved by the amount the mean load requires.
proposed_change: Added an oscillation-aware load estimator: it builds the instantaneous load residual over the whole telemetry window and, when that residual reverses sign three or more times about its median (a sustained oscillation), replaces the single-sample load with the residual median so the split stops chasing the oscillation; otherwise the instantaneous residual is kept so steps are followed at once.

failure_analysis.what_failed: On oscillating disturbances the supervisor estimates the load from the single last sample, so its setpoint bias follows the oscillation with the ~1.5-2 min loop/settling lag. The resulting moves land in the WRONG direction (e.g. sp_h2 lowered while feed2 is already draining tank2, sp_h1 raised while h3 is climbing), which both injects large production transients (Q depends only on the setpoints at steady state, so every needless move is pure off-target production) and drives h2 out of band and h3 above 0.75 when v2 saturates. The prior moving-average/LPF attempts failed because they also slowed the response to genuine steps, so h3 blew up on fresh feed steps.
failure_analysis.next_recommendation: Keep the instantaneous residual for steps but blend it toward the multi-period window mean whenever the recent residual repeatedly changes sign (oscillation), so the outer loop stops chasing the AC component without losing step authority.

self_check: The load estimate used by the split optimizer is instantaneous when the recent mass-balance residual keeps one sign (a step or ramp), so a fresh feed/pump/split step still shifts production fast enough to keep v2 off its 12 V rail and h3 under 0.75. When the residual flips sign repeatedly (an oscillation), the estimate is blended toward the full-window mean, which is the lag-free DC load, so the setpoints stay put and Q stays on target instead of chasing the oscillation out of phase. Because Q at steady state equals the flow implied by the two setpoints, holding the setpoints through a zero-mean oscillation removes the largest production-error term, and the only moves left are those genuinely needed to relieve a predicted constraint. Constraint predictions (h3p, h4p, h2p, v1p, v2p) still use the loaded model, so any residual AC leakage is bounded and never pushes the loop into saturation.
proposed_change: Replace the single-sample load residual (d1,d2) with an oscillation-aware estimate that blends the instantaneous residual toward the multi-period window mean when the recent residual sign flips (oscillation) but keeps it instantaneous when the sign persists (step).

failure_analysis.what_failed: The worst scores are the few-minute sinusoidal feed disturbances (dev_feed_sine_2 1659, dev_feed_sine_1 872, dev_combined_sine_1 872). The supervisor infers the instantaneous pump flows A=0.8*k1*v1 and B=0.8*k2*v2 from the upper-tank drains f4=a4*sqrt(2g*h4) and f3=a3*sqrt(2g*h3). Those drains only equal the pump flows at steady state; with the upper tanks' ~100 s time constants they lag the true flows by roughly a third of the oscillation period. The resulting load estimate d1,d2 is out of phase, so the split correction is applied late (trace: at t=810 the estimated d2 is about -1.5 L/s while the true feed2 is -2.45 L/s, and the supervisor keeps h2_sp near 0.27 instead of the feasible ~0.22), production rides +-1.5 L/s off target and h2/h3 sit on the band and upper limits (272 s band, 123 s upper for dev_feed_sine_2).
failure_analysis.next_recommendation: Keep the accumulation-corrected load estimate (f3+dh3/dt, f4+dh4/dt) for d1,d2 only, and keep the steady-state f3,f4 for the pump-gain estimates k1e,k2e, so the estimator lag is removed without corrupting the voltage predictions (the loss mechanism of the gen-2 c1 dynamic estimate).

self_check: The split is chosen by evaluating the steady-state relation q1+q2=Q, A=(4Q2-Q1)/3, B=(4Q1-Q2)/3 for every candidate q1 with the accumulation-corrected load d1,d2, so when a feed disturbance pushes an upper level toward its limit or a pump toward saturation the cost (3000 per m above the upper target, 3000 per m outside the h2 band, 2000 per V above 12 V) immediately moves the pair along the constant-Q curve away from that corner. Because d1,d2 now include the upper-tank accumulation dh3/dt, dh4/dt, the estimate is in phase with the disturbance instead of ~100 s behind, so the corrective split is applied while the disturbance is still acting rather than after it has reversed; production therefore stays on target and the levels do not ride the band and upper-level edges for as many seconds. The static f3,f4 are still used for k1e,k2e, and the 45 s post-change hold plus the 0.06 m step limit keep the setpoint travel from being spent on the inner-loop transient.
proposed_change: Replace the single-sample steady-state load estimate (d1,d2 from f3,f4) with an accumulation-corrected one using f3+dh3/dt and f4+dh4/dt, while leaving the pump-gain estimates k1e,k2e on the original static f3,f4.

failure_analysis.what_failed: The load estimate used for the split assumes the upper tanks are in equilibrium, so it ignores the lower-tank level rate. During an oscillating feed the estimate lags the true disturbance by ~100 s (e.g. at t=430 in dev_feed_sine_2 the true d2 is -1.84 L/s but the estimate is -0.17 L/s), so the supervisor keeps h2 high and h1 low while tank2 is being drawn down; it then shifts the split only after the disturbance has reversed. The wrong-direction split saturates v1, drops Q to ~15 L/s and pushes h2 out of the band (feed_sine_2 1659, combined_sine_1 872, feed_sine_1 872).
failure_analysis.next_recommendation: Keep the gate; if churn reappears, also stop the pump-gain estimate from dipping whenever an upper tank fills (k1e currently collapses to Am/v1 during transients and makes the optimizer avoid the pump that is actually needed).

self_check: The split is chosen from the exact tank balance, so as soon as a disturbance makes a lower level move away from its setpoint the estimated load includes that level rate and the constant-Q split is shifted toward the other tank without lag; when an upper level or a pump approaches its limit the same model penalises the predicted h3/h4 above the limit and the predicted voltage above 12 V, so the optimiser keeps the split inside the safe region. The rate term is applied only while a level moves away from its setpoint, so the loop's own response to a setpoint change is never mistaken for a load and the supervisor does not fight its own command. Because both setpoints stay on the constant-Q curve the production target is unchanged by the bias, and the 0.06 m step limit plus the 45 s transient hold keep the travel small.
proposed_change: Add the measured lower-tank level rate to the steady-state load estimate so the split uses the instantaneous disturbance, gated so the rate is added only while that level is moving away from its setpoint.

failure_analysis.what_failed: The supervisor re-evaluates constraints only 45 s after its own setpoint change, but the PI loops and the 1-1.5 V voltage overshoot take 70-115 s to settle, so the levels/slopes/voltages it reads are its own transient, not the disturbance. It then estimates a bogus load/pump gain and issues another corrective split move, which creates a fresh transient - a perpetual chase that produces most of the production off-target, setpoint travel and band/upper-level violations on sinusoidal feed/combined disturbances.
failure_analysis.next_recommendation: Extend the post-setpoint-change settling hold past the loop settling and voltage-overshoot time so the split decision is made only on settled measurements, breaking the self-induced chase without slowing the one-off response to a genuine target change.

self_check: Production stays on target because the two PI loops hold h1 and h2 at the pair of setpoints the supervisor returns, so Q = a1*sqrt(2g*h1)+a2*sqrt(2g*h2) equals the target independent of the split. The one change lengthens the hold after every setpoint move to 100 s, so the supervisor no longer mistakes its own loop transient (and the 1-1.5 V voltage overshoot) for a disturbance and stops chasing oscillations with repeated split moves, which is what drove the h2 band and h3/h4 limit violations. Because the constant-Q constraint is enforced for every candidate split, the h1/h2 pair always recombines to the target, while the split-search penalties still bias away from splits that push h3/h4 over the limit or the pumps toward saturation.
proposed_change: Extend the post-setpoint-change settling hold from 45 s to 100 s so the supervisor only re-optimizes the split after the PI loops and their voltage overshoot have settled, instead of reacting to its own transient.
